paper.title: Evaluation of exposure-specific risks from two independent samples: a simulation study
paper.citation: Reichmann WM, Gagnon D, Horsburgh CR, Losina E. Evaluation of exposure-specific risks from two independent samples: a simulation study. BMC Medical Research Methodology 11:1 (2011)

items.label: Table 1, the parameter grid

cause.summary: The design of the simulation (P(E), P(D|not E), RR, N1/N2); used as input, nothing to compare.

items.label: Table 2, relative bias of ESR_S and ESR_R (1000/1000 and 5000/5000)
items.notes: Table 2 prints -0.8% for ESR_S, Scenario 4, RR 1.0, 1000/1000; Table S1 prints 0.8%. Ours, 1.4%, is within tolerance of both.

assumptions.what: The 'assumed population ESR' is RR x P(D|not E) unrounded (0.135 for the label .14), not the rounded label of the tables
assumptions.sensitivity: The rounded label leaves 102 of 112 cells of Table S1 and 101 of S2 within tolerance (RMS z 1.972 and 2.277 against 1.139 and 1.168); the population's realized ESR gives the same as RR x P(D|not E) (RMS z 1.123 and 1.154). comparison.json, hypotheses.

assumptions.what: When sample 2 has no cases among its exposed (or its unexposed), the log interval is (0, infinity): it covers, and it has no finite length, so it is left out of the expected length. The paper does not say.
assumptions.sensitivity: Leaving those intervals out of the coverage instead (missing) gives Table S5 RMS z 1.144 against 1.08, and in Scenario 1 at N2 = 1000 puts our coverage below the paper's on average in two runs (mean z -0.66 and -0.98 over those 14 cells); counting them as not covering leaves 101 of 112 S5 cells within (RMS z 4.061); adding 0.5 to the cells leaves 107 of 112 S7 cells within (RMS z 2.638). Only Scenario 1 at N2 = 1000 has many such pairs (up to 39%); the 250/250 runs have at most 1%.

assumptions.what: One population of 10 million per setting, by Bernoulli draws of exposure and disease; both samples drawn from it without replacement, independently of each other; 1,000 pairs per setting; our own seeds
assumptions.sensitivity: Exact cell proportions instead of draws change nothing (Tables S1, S2, S5, S7 112 of 112 each, exact_population in comparison.json). The seeds are ours: two runs of ours differ by more than the tolerance in 8 of 784 cells.

assumptions.what: Comparison tolerance: half a printed unit plus 3 x sqrt(2) Monte Carlo standard errors of one 1,000-pair estimate, fixed before the comparison
assumptions.sensitivity: With it two runs of our own design agree in 776 of 784 cells (99.0%). Wrong inputs (scenario or N1/N2 swapped) fall outside in 21% to 81% of the cells of Tables S1, S3, S5, S6 and S7; in Tables S2 and S4, where the true bias is 0 everywhere, a wrong input is almost as good as a right one.

cause.summary: Monte Carlo error: the paper's seeds are not given, and two runs of our own design differ by more than the tolerance in 8 of 784 cells (1.0%). Our second run, with another seed, puts each of these cells within tolerance.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The cell is a chance miss of our run
hypotheses.test: The same design with another seed (replicate in comparison.json)

hypotheses.hypothesis: A systematic difference in the setting
hypotheses.test: The RMS z of the tables with a chance miss is 0.97 to 1.27, near the 1 expected of Monte Carlo error alone

cause.summary: The paper's log CI of ESR_R behaves as if the first term of eq. 10, the variance of ln P1(D|not E), had been left out of the simulation (or computed as p(1-p)/n1, the variance of the proportion rather than of its log, which is close to 0). With eq. 10 as printed, our intervals cover more often, most of all at N1/N2 1000/5000 where that term is largest; without it, 112 of 112 cells of Table S6 (against 82 with it) and 47 of 47 bars of Figs 1-4 come back. The case study (Table 5) used eq. 10 as printed. The SAS code is lost, so this is read from the results.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The first term of eq. 10 is left out
hypotheses.test: Same samples, log CI of ESR_R without (1 - P1(D|not E)) / (n1 P1(D|not E)): Table S6 112 of 112 (RMS z 0.993, against 4.297 as printed)

hypotheses.hypothesis: The first term is P1(D|not E)(1 - P1(D|not E))/n1, the variance of the proportion
hypotheses.test: Same samples with that term: Table S6 112 of 112

hypotheses.hypothesis: n2 is used in place of n1 in the first term
hypotheses.test: Same samples with n2: Table S6 99 of 112

hypotheses.hypothesis: P1(D) is used in place of P1(D|not E) in the first term
hypotheses.test: Same samples with P1(D): Table S6 83 of 112

hypotheses.hypothesis: Zero cells handled another way
hypotheses.test: Missing, not covering, or 0.5 added: Table S6 stays at 72 to 82 of 112

hypotheses.hypothesis: The case study used the same shortened variance
hypotheses.test: Table 5: n1 solved from the binomial CI and Var(ln RR2) from the CI of ESR_S; the log CI of ESR_R predicted with and without the first term
